slides.title: Biology — Mitosis and the Cell Division Process
slides.purpose: Step through Interphase, Mitosis (PMAT), and Cytokinesis with consistent diploid chromosome count (2n = 4).
onScreenText: Interphase precedes mitosis; cytokinesis completes division
Diploid count remains 2n = 4 in each daughter cell
Chromatid separation halves chromatids, not chromosome count

visual.altText: Mitosis and cell division overview showing 2n = 4 parent cell forming two 2n = 4 daughter cells
visual.svgCode: <svg viewBox="0 0 800 450" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect width="800" height="450" fill="#f5f3ff"/><text x="400" y="205" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="34" font-weight="bold" fill="#4c1d95">Mitosis & Cell Division (2n = 4)</text><text x="400" y="258" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#6d28d9">Interphase → Prophase → Metaphase → Anaphase → Telophase → Cytokinesis</text></svg>

narration.script: Step through how a diploid cell with four chromosomes replicates its DNA during interphase, separates sister chromatids during mitosis, and divides its cytoplasm in cytokinesis.

keyIdeas: Interphase precedes mitosis; cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm and may overlap late telophase.

interactive.title: Mitosis and the Cell Division Process
interactive.instructions: Step through all six stages for a model diploid cell (2n = 4) and track how DNA, chromatids, and the nuclear membrane change.
interactive.accessibilityLabel: Interactive six-stage mitosis and cell division stepper
interactive.fallbackText: Interphase replicates DNA before mitosis. Prophase condenses chromosomes, Metaphase aligns them at the equator, Anaphase separates sister chromatids, Telophase reforms nuclei, and Cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm into two identical 2n = 4 daughter cells.
interactive.modelNote: Interphase precedes mitosis; cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm and may overlap late mitosis. Model diploid count: 2n = 4.

stages.title: Interphase (Preparation)
stages.summary: Before mitosis begins, the cell grows and replicates its DNA during S phase so each of the 4 chromosomes consists of two identical sister chromatids.
stages.startingCondition: 4 unreplicated chromosomes (4 chromatids) inside an intact nucleus.
stages.whatChanges: DNA replicates; chromatid count doubles from 4 to 8 while chromosome count stays 4.
stages.whyItMatters: Guarantees both daughter cells inherit an exact, complete copy of the genome.
stages.connectionToNext: Once DNA replication and growth checkpoints pass, the cell enters Prophase.
stages.commonMisconception: Interphase is NOT a stage of mitosis—it prepares the cell before mitosis starts.

stages.title: Prophase
stages.summary: Chromatin condenses into visible X-shaped chromosomes (each with two sister chromatids), spindle fibres form, and the nuclear membrane breaks down.
stages.whatChanges: Chromosomes thicken and become visible; nuclear membrane disintegrates.
stages.whyItMatters: Condensing DNA prevents tangling or breaking during movement.
stages.connectionToNext: Spindle fibres attach to centromeres to guide chromosomes to the equator.

stages.title: Metaphase
stages.summary: Spindle fibres align all 4 chromosomes single-file along the cell equator (metaphase plate).
stages.whatChanges: Chromosomes line up centrally with spindle fibres attached to opposite sides of each centromere.
stages.whyItMatters: Ensures each pole receives exactly one sister chromatid from every chromosome.
stages.connectionToNext: Once alignment is checked, centromeres split to start Anaphase.

prediction.prompt: What happens immediately after chromosomes align at the cell equator?
options: Sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles
The nuclear membrane thickens around the equator
prediction.explanation: In Anaphase, centromeres divide and spindle fibres pull sister chromatids to opposite poles.

stages.title: Anaphase
stages.summary: Centromeres split and shortening spindle fibres pull sister chromatids to opposite poles; each separated chromatid is now an individual chromosome.
stages.whatChanges: 4 chromosomes move to the left pole and 4 identical chromosomes move to the right pole.
stages.whyItMatters: Physically divides the duplicated genetic material equally.
stages.connectionToNext: When chromosomes arrive at the poles, Telophase begins.

stages.title: Telophase
stages.summary: Two new nuclear membranes form around the two clusters of 4 chromosomes, which decondense back into chromatin.
stages.whatChanges: Nuclear division (mitosis) completes; two genetically identical nuclei exist in one cell.
stages.connectionToNext: Cytokinesis (which often starts during late telophase) separates the cytoplasm.

stages.title: Cytokinesis
stages.summary: The cytoplasm divides (cleavage furrow in animals; cell plate in plants), producing two separate, genetically identical diploid daughter cells.
stages.whatChanges: One parent cell becomes two independent daughter cells.
stages.whyItMatters: Completes cell division for growth and tissue repair.

sequenceChallenge.prompt: Arrange the four core phases of mitosis (nuclear division) in the correct order.
sequenceChallenge.explanation: Nuclear division follows PMAT: Prophase (condense) → Metaphase (align) → Anaphase (separate) → Telophase (reform nuclei).

slides.title: Computer Science — CPU Fetch–Decode–Execute Cycle
slides.purpose: Trace a specific simplified instruction (LOAD 5 at address 100) through PC, MAR, MDR, CIR, and ACC.
onScreenText: Example instruction: LOAD 5 stored at address 100
Tracks PC, MAR, MDR, CIR, and ACC registers live
Not every instruction requires the ALU

visual.altText: CPU Fetch Decode Execute register schematic
visual.svgCode: <svg viewBox="0 0 800 450" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect width="800" height="450" fill="#0f172a"/><text x="400" y="205" text-anchor="middle" font-family="monospace" font-size="34" font-weight="bold" fill="#38bdf8">Fetch → Decode → Execute</text><text x="400" y="258" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#94a3b8">Trace LOAD 5 (address 100) across PC, MAR, MDR, CIR, and ACC</text></svg>

narration.script: Trace how a simplified accumulator processor fetches, decodes, and executes the instruction LOAD 5 stored at memory address 100.

keyIdeas: PC increments during fetch; LOAD transfers data into ACC without needing an ALU calculation.

interactive.title: CPU Fetch–Decode–Execute Cycle (Example: LOAD 5)
interactive.instructions: Step through the registers as the CPU executes LOAD 5 (stored at address 100, where memory[5] holds value 42).
interactive.accessibilityLabel: Interactive CPU Fetch Decode Execute register stepper
interactive.fallbackText: PC (100) copies to MAR; memory[100] ('LOAD 5') loads into MDR then CIR; PC increments to 101; Control Unit decodes LOAD 5; Execute reads memory[5] (42) into ACC.
interactive.modelNote: Simplified single-accumulator Von Neumann model executing LOAD 5. Not all instructions pass through the ALU (LOAD transfers memory to ACC directly). Restarting the cycle replays this LOAD 5 example rather than fetching address 101.

stages.title: Fetch 1: Copy PC to MAR
stages.summary: The address of the next instruction (100) is copied from the Program Counter (PC) into the Memory Address Register (MAR).
stages.whatChanges: MAR receives address 100 and places it on the address bus.

stages.title: Fetch 2: Read Instruction & Increment PC
stages.summary: Main memory returns the instruction at address 100 ('LOAD 5') into the MDR while the PC increments to 101.
stages.whatChanges: MDR holds 'LOAD 5'; PC advances to 101 ready for the next instruction.

stages.title: Fetch 3: Transfer MDR to CIR
stages.summary: The fetched instruction is copied from the MDR into the Current Instruction Register (CIR).
stages.whatChanges: CIR now holds 'LOAD 5', freeing MDR for operand data transfers.

stages.title: Decode Instruction
stages.summary: The Control Unit decodes 'LOAD 5' into opcode LOAD (read from memory into ACC) and operand address 5.
stages.whatChanges: Control signals prepare to read data from address 5 (ALU arithmetic is NOT needed for LOAD).

prediction.prompt: Which unit decodes the instruction inside the CIR?
prediction.explanation: The Control Unit decodes the opcode and operand in the CIR and generates control signals.

stages.title: Execute LOAD 5
stages.summary: Memory address 5 returns value 42 into the MDR, which is then loaded into the Accumulator (ACC).
stages.whatChanges: ACC updates from 0 to 42; the CPU is now ready to fetch the next instruction at PC = 101.

slides.title: NaCCA Science — The Water Cycle (Simplified Pathway)
slides.purpose: Explore a cyclic natural mechanism tracking state of matter and thermal energy transfer.
onScreenText: Simplified 4-stage cyclic pathway
Tracks state of matter & thermal energy
Real water molecules take many interconnected paths

visual.svgCode: <svg viewBox="0 0 800 450" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect width="800" height="450" fill="#e0f2fe"/><text x="400" y="205" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="36" font-weight="bold" fill="#0c4a6e">The Water Cycle</text><text x="400" y="258" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#0369a1">Evaporation → Condensation → Precipitation → Collection</text></svg>

narration.script: Follow one simplified pathway of water through evaporation, condensation, precipitation, and collection, tracking how thermal energy drives each change of state.

keyIdeas: Solar thermal energy drives evaporation; cooling aloft causes condensation.

interactive.title: The Water Cycle (Simplified Pathway)
interactive.instructions: Step around this cyclic pathway and observe how water changes state and exchanges heat energy.
interactive.fallbackText: Solar heat causes evaporation (liquid to vapour), cooling causes condensation (vapour to droplets forming clouds), gravity drives precipitation, and runoff/infiltration returns water to collection bodies.
interactive.modelNote: This 4-stage loop is a simplified pathway within a larger interconnected natural cycle—not every water molecule follows the same four stages in order (some evaporate again immediately or remain in groundwater/glaciers).

stages.title: Evaporation
stages.summary: Thermal energy from the Sun warms surface water in rivers, lakes, and oceans, turning liquid water into invisible water vapour that rises.
stages.whatChanges: Liquid water absorbs heat and changes into gas (water vapour).

stages.title: Condensation
stages.summary: As warm water vapour rises into cooler upper air, it loses thermal energy and condenses into tiny liquid droplets around dust particles, forming clouds.
stages.whatChanges: Water vapour releases heat and turns back into liquid droplets.

stages.title: Precipitation
stages.summary: Cloud droplets combine until they become too heavy to stay suspended, falling to Earth as rain (or hail/snow in cold regions).
stages.whatChanges: Gravity pulls heavy water droplets downward to land and sea.

stages.title: Collection & Runoff
stages.summary: Rainwater flows over land as surface runoff or infiltrates into soil and groundwater, collecting in rivers, lakes, and oceans.
stages.whatChanges: Water returns to surface reservoirs and underground aquifers.

sequenceChallenge.prompt: Order this simplified 4-stage water pathway starting from solar warming of ocean water.
sequenceChallenge.explanation: Evaporation lifts vapour → Condensation forms clouds → Precipitation falls → Collection returns water to reservoirs.

slides.title: Chemistry — Electrolysis of Molten Lead(II) Bromide
slides.purpose: Trace ion mobility, concurrent reduction at cathode and oxidation at anode with safety context.
onScreenText: Conceptual virtual demo (PbBr₂ is toxic)
Cathode (-): Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Pb (reduction)
Anode (+): 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻ (oxidation, concurrent)

visual.altText: Electrolysis of molten lead(II) bromide electrode half-equations
visual.svgCode: <svg viewBox="0 0 800 450" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect width="800" height="450" fill="#fff7ed"/><text x="400" y="205" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="32" font-weight="bold" fill="#9a3412">Electrolysis of Molten PbBr₂</text><text x="400" y="258" text-anchor="middle" font-family="monospace" font-size="20" fill="#c2410c">Cathode: Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Pb · Anode: 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻</text></svg>

narration.script: Examine this conceptual virtual demonstration of electrolysing molten lead two bromide. Remember that reduction at the cathode and oxidation at the anode happen at the same time.

keyIdeas: Ions must be free to move (molten); oxidation at anode and reduction at cathode occur concurrently.

interactive.title: Electrolysis of Molten Lead(II) Bromide (Virtual Model)
interactive.instructions: Step through how melting frees ions and how opposite electrodes drive concurrent redox reactions.
interactive.accessibilityLabel: Electrolysis of molten lead II bromide four-stage stepper
interactive.fallbackText: Solid PbBr2 cannot conduct because ions are fixed. Melting frees Pb2+ and Br- ions. Under DC voltage, Pb2+ is reduced to molten lead at the negative cathode while Br- is simultaneously oxidised to brown bromine vapour at the positive anode.
interactive.modelNote: Conceptual virtual demonstration only—lead(II) bromide and bromine vapour are toxic and corrosive, so this is NOT an independent student practical (teacher fume-cupboard demonstration only). Cathode reduction and anode oxidation occur concurrently.

stages.title: Solid Ionic Lattice (No Conduction)
stages.summary: At room temperature, Pb²⁺ and Br⁻ ions are locked in a rigid ionic lattice and cannot move to carry charge.

stages.title: Heating to Melt PbBr₂
stages.summary: Heating above 373 °C melts the solid, breaking the rigid lattice so Pb²⁺ cations and Br⁻ anions move freely.
stages.whatChanges: Free-moving ions make the molten salt an electrical conductor (electrolyte).

stages.title: DC Power Applied: Ion Migration
stages.summary: Applying DC voltage attracts positive Pb²⁺ ions toward the negative cathode and negative Br⁻ ions toward the positive anode.

prediction.prompt: Which ion moves to the positive electrode (anode) and what happens to it?
options: Br⁻ moves to the anode and loses electrons (oxidation)
Pb²⁺ moves to the anode and gains electrons
Br⁻ moves to the cathode and gains electrons
prediction.explanation: Opposites attract: negative Br⁻ ions migrate to the positive anode and lose electrons (oxidation) to form Br₂.

stages.title: Concurrent Cathode & Anode Reactions
stages.summary: Reduction and oxidation occur simultaneously: at the cathode Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Pb (silvery molten lead); at the anode 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻ (brown bromine vapour).
stages.whyItMatters: Electrons removed at the anode flow through the external circuit to the cathode, balancing charge continuously.

slides.title: Biology — Human Digestion Pathway
slides.purpose: Distinguish mechanical digestion, chemical digestion, absorption, and egestion across organs.
onScreenText: Mechanical vs chemical digestion distinguished
Absorption happens mainly in the small intestine
Egestion removes undigested waste (not excretion)

visual.svgCode: <svg viewBox="0 0 800 450" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect width="800" height="450" fill="#f0fdf4"/><text x="400" y="205" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="36" font-weight="bold" fill="#14532d">Human Digestion Pathway</text><text x="400" y="258" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#166534">Mechanical · Chemical · Absorption · Egestion</text></svg>

narration.script: Follow a meal from the mouth to egestion, noting where mechanical breakdown, enzymatic chemical digestion, and nutrient absorption take place.

keyIdeas: Absorption occurs primarily across villi in the small intestine; egestion removes undigested solids.

interactive.title: Human Digestion Pathway
interactive.instructions: Step through each organ to distinguish mechanical digestion, chemical digestion, absorption, and egestion.
interactive.fallbackText: Mouth chews food and starts starch digestion (amylase); Stomach churns food with acid and protease; Small Intestine completes chemical digestion and absorbs nutrients via villi; Large Intestine absorbs water; Rectum stores and egests undigested faeces.

stages.title: Mouth (Ingestion & Early Digestion)
stages.summary: Teeth chew food into smaller pieces (mechanical digestion) while salivary amylase begins breaking starch into maltose (chemical digestion).

stages.title: Stomach
stages.summary: Muscular walls churn food (mechanical) while hydrochloric acid kills pathogens and provides acidic pH for pepsin (protease) to begin protein digestion.

stages.title: Small Intestine (Digestion & Absorption)
stages.summary: Bile emulsifies fats; pancreatic and intestinal enzymes complete chemical digestion into glucose, amino acids, fatty acids, and glycerol, which absorb through villi into the bloodstream.

stages.title: Large Intestine (Water Absorption)
stages.summary: Remaining water and mineral ions are absorbed from undigested material, forming semi-solid faeces.

stages.title: Rectum & Anus (Egestion)
stages.summary: Undigested food waste (faeces) is stored in the rectum and expelled through the anus—this is egestion.
stages.commonMisconception: Egestion (removing undigested food) is different from excretion (removing metabolic waste like urea and CO₂).

slides.title: Computer Science — Binary Search Step Trace
slides.purpose: Trace binary search on sorted array [4, 11, 18, 25, 33, 42, 57] for target 42 with explicit midpoint convention.
onScreenText: Target: 42 · Midpoint: floor((low + high) / 2)
Halves remaining search space each step

visual.altText: Sorted array indices 0 to 6 for binary search trace
visual.svgCode: <svg viewBox="0 0 800 450" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect width="800" height="450" fill="#0f172a"/><text x="400" y="205" text-anchor="middle" font-family="monospace" font-size="30" font-weight="bold" fill="#34d399">[4, 11, 18, 25, 33, 42, 57]</text><text x="400" y="258" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#94a3b8">Target = 42 · mid = floor((low + high) / 2)</text></svg>

narration.script: Trace binary search looking for 42 in a seven-element sorted array. Watch how low, mid, and high narrow the search range in just two comparisons.

keyIdeas: Binary search requires a sorted array and discards half the elements on each comparison.

interactive.title: Binary Search Trace (Target = 42)
interactive.instructions: Step through the pointer updates (low, mid, high) as binary search locates 42 inside [4, 11, 18, 25, 33, 42, 57].
interactive.accessibilityLabel: Binary search four-stage pointer trace stepper
interactive.fallbackText: Start with low=0, high=6. Mid=3 gives 25 < 42, so set low=4. Next mid=floor((4+6)/2)=5 gives 42 == 42: target found at index 5.
interactive.modelNote: 0-based indexing on sorted array [4, 11, 18, 25, 33, 42, 57]; integer midpoint convention: mid = floor((low + high) / 2). Terminates when array[mid] == target or low > high (not found).

stages.title: Initialise Search Bounds
stages.summary: Set low = 0 and high = 6 to cover all 7 sorted elements [4, 11, 18, 25, 33, 42, 57].

stages.title: Comparison 1: Inspect mid = 3
stages.summary: Compute mid = floor((0 + 6) / 2) = 3. Compare array[3] = 25 with target 42: since 25 < 42, 42 cannot be in indices 0..3.
stages.whatChanges: Half the array (indices 0..3) is eliminated in one comparison.

stages.title: Narrow Bounds: low ← mid + 1
stages.summary: Move low to mid + 1 = 4 so the active search range becomes indices 4..6 ([33, 42, 57]).

stages.title: Comparison 2: Inspect mid = 5 (Found!)
stages.summary: Compute mid = floor((4 + 6) / 2) = 5. Compare array[5] = 42 with target 42: exact match! Algorithm terminates returning index 5.

slides.title: Mathematics — Solving a Linear Equation (3x + 5 = 20)
slides.purpose: Explain why each inverse algebraic operation is applied while preserving equality at every step.
onScreenText: Equation: 3x + 5 = 20
Apply the same inverse operation to both sides
Check solution by substituting x = 5 back in

visual.svgCode: <svg viewBox="0 0 800 450" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect width="800" height="450" fill="#f8fafc"/><text x="400" y="205" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="44" font-weight="bold" fill="#0f172a">3x + 5 = 20</text><text x="400" y="260" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#0284c7">Preserve equality at every inverse step</text></svg>

narration.script: Step through solving three x plus five equals twenty, seeing why each inverse operation keeps both sides balanced.

keyIdeas: Doing the same operation to both sides preserves equality.

interactive.title: Solving 3x + 5 = 20 (Preserving Equality)
interactive.instructions: Step through each algebraic transformation and observe how both sides stay equal.
interactive.fallbackText: Start with 3x + 5 = 20. Subtract 5 from both sides to get 3x = 15. Divide both sides by 3 to get x = 5. Substitute back: 3(5) + 5 = 20.

stages.title: Original Equation
stages.summary: We want to isolate x. Currently x is multiplied by 3 and then 5 is added.

stages.title: Subtract 5 from Both Sides
stages.summary: Undo '+ 5' by subtracting 5 from both sides: (3x + 5) − 5 = 20 − 5, giving 3x = 15.
stages.whyItMatters: Subtracting the same value from both sides preserves equality.

stages.title: Divide Both Sides by 3
stages.summary: Undo '× 3' by dividing both sides by 3: 3x / 3 = 15 / 3, giving x = 5.

stages.title: Verify by Substitution
stages.summary: Substitute x = 5 into 3x + 5: 3(5) + 5 = 15 + 5 = 20, matching the right-hand side.

slides.title: A-Level Chemistry — Electrophilic Addition (Ethene + HBr)
slides.purpose: Trace electron-pair movement, π-bond cleavage, carbocation intermediate, and nucleophilic attack.
onScreenText: Electron-rich C=C π bond attacks δ⁺ H of HBr
Heterolytic fission forms carbocation + Br⁻
Br⁻ lone pair forms C–Br bond → bromoethane

visual.altText: Electrophilic addition of HBr to ethene forming bromoethane
visual.svgCode: <svg viewBox="0 0 800 450" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect width="800" height="450" fill="#fdf2f8"/><text x="400" y="205" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="32" font-weight="bold" fill="#831843">Electrophilic Addition: C₂H₄ + HBr</text><text x="400" y="258" text-anchor="middle" font-family="monospace" font-size="20" fill="#9d174d">CH₂=CH₂ + H–Br → [CH₃–CH₂⁺] + Br⁻ → CH₃CH₂Br</text></svg>

narration.script: Trace how the electron-rich pi bond of ethene attacks the partially positive hydrogen of hydrogen bromide to form a carbocation intermediate and then bromoethane.

keyIdeas: Curly arrows always show the movement of an electron pair from electron-rich to electron-deficient sites.

interactive.title: Electrophilic Addition of HBr to Ethene
interactive.instructions: Step through electron-pair movement, bond breaking/forming, and intermediate formation.
interactive.fallbackText: Ethene's C=C pi bond attacks the delta-positive H of polar HBr; the H-Br bond breaks heterolytically to yield an ethyl carbocation (CH3CH2+) and Br-; finally Br- donates a lone pair to the positive carbon to form bromoethane (CH3CH2Br).

stages.title: Polarised Electrophile Approaches π Bond
stages.summary: HBr is permanently polar (Hδ⁺–Brδ⁻) because Br is more electronegative than H. It approaches the high electron density of ethene's C=C π bond.

stages.title: π-Bond Attack & Heterolytic Fission
stages.summary: A pair of electrons from the C=C π bond forms a new C–H σ bond with Hδ⁺. Simultaneously, the H–Br bond breaks heterolytically, sending both bonding electrons onto Br.

prediction.prompt: What intermediate ion is formed when the π bond forms a C–H bond and Br⁻ departs?
prediction.explanation: The second carbon loses its share of the π electrons, leaving a positively charged ethyl carbocation (CH₃–CH₂⁺).

stages.title: Carbocation Intermediate & Br⁻ Nucleophile
stages.summary: An unstable, positively charged ethyl carbocation intermediate (CH₃–CH₂⁺) exists briefly alongside the bromide ion (:Br⁻) carrying a lone pair.

stages.title: Nucleophilic Attack → Bromoethane
stages.summary: The bromide ion donates a lone pair of electrons to the positively charged carbon, forming a C–Br covalent bond and yielding saturated bromoethane (CH₃CH₂Br).
